words.definition: to accept or agree to something without protest
words.origin: Latin acquiescere, to rest or remain quiet
words.mnemonic: A C before the Q, and an S-C near the end: ac-qui-esce.
sentences: After a long debate, the board chose to acquiesce to the new plan.
She would not acquiesce just because everyone else agreed.

words.definition: to make something bad or unsatisfactory better
words.mnemonic: Hide the Latin melior (better) inside: a-melior-ate.
sentences: New bike lanes helped ameliorate traffic downtown.
Nothing could ameliorate the sting of losing in the final round.

words.definition: something that belongs to a different time period
words.origin: Greek ana, against, and khronos, time
words.mnemonic: Chronos is time, spelled with CH, as in chronological.
sentences: A wristwatch on a Roman soldier is an obvious anachronism.
The fax machine in the office felt like an anachronism.

words.definition: hostile and eager to fight or argue
sentences: The belligerent customer shouted at every employee.
His tone turned belligerent as soon as he lost the argument.

words.definition: changing mood or behavior suddenly and without reason
sentences: Spring weather here is capricious, so pack an umbrella.
The capricious manager changed the deadline three times.

words.definition: an expert judge in matters of taste, such as food or art
words.mnemonic: Double N, double S, and a French -eur ending.
sentences: A true connoisseur can name the coffee bean by taste alone.
He became a connoisseur of street food while traveling.

words.definition: careful to do one's work or duty well
sentences: A conscientious student double-checks every answer.
She is conscientious about replying to every email.

words.definition: a person who dabbles in a subject without real commitment
words.mnemonic: One L, then a double T: dil-et-tante.
sentences: He is a dilettante who starts a new hobby every month.
Critics dismissed her as a dilettante, but her paintings sold out.

words.origin: Latin egregius, standing out from the flock
words.mnemonic: E-GREG-ious: Greg stood out from the flock, for the wrong reasons.
sentences: Charging twenty dollars for water is an egregious markup.
The referee made an egregious call in the final minute.

words.definition: a habit or way of behaving that is peculiar to one person
words.origin: Greek idios, own, and synkrasis, mixture
words.mnemonic: It ends in -crasy, not -cracy like democracy.
sentences: Humming while she reads is her strangest idiosyncrasy.
Every old house has some idiosyncrasy, like a door that sticks.

words.origin: Latin mel, honey, and fluere, to flow
sentences: The narrator's mellifluous voice made the audiobook a joy.
A mellifluous melody drifted out of the cafe.

words.definition: done secretly because it would not be approved of
words.mnemonic: Double R, then a single P sneaks in quietly.
sentences: He took a surreptitious glance at his phone during the meeting.
Their surreptitious snack run went unnoticed.
